1.title: AI Foundations: What AI Is, Its Harms and Its Principles
1.text: Welcome to Module one: A I Foundations. This module covers domain one, competency A, of the Body of Knowledge. You will learn what A I is, what can go wrong with it, why it needs its own kind of governance, and the principles that guide responsible use. It is the vocabulary for everything that follows.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Define A I and tell its main types apart. Separate an A I model, an A I system, and a general-purpose A I model. Name the harms and risks that A I poses to people, groups, organizations and society. Explain the characteristics that make A I need its own governance. And apply the common principles of responsible A I, including where they conflict.

1.title: Case Check-In: Two Kinds of AI at Helios
1.text: At Helios, two leaders own two different systems. Lucia Moreno, Head of Talent Acquisition, owns the hiring tool, which predicts which applicants fit a role. Anika Berg, the Customer Support director, owns the assistant, which generates answers to customer questions. Samira Haddad asks you whether these are the same kind of A I, and what can go wrong with each. Your answers will set the scope of the governance program.

1.title: Defining AI: Four Sources, One Core
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The Body of Knowledge asks for the generally accepted definitions, so here are four. The core idea is shared: a machine-based system that, for given objectives, generates outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations or decisions. The O E C D, short for Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, and the E U A I Act, in Article three, point one, add that objectives may be explicit or implicit, and that autonomy and adaptiveness vary. N I S T, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, adapts the same wording. The International Organization for Standardization, I S O, standard twenty-two nine eight nine, speaks of human-defined objectives; that depth comes from public summaries. Exam tip: expect the shared core.

1.title: Types of AI: Nested Families
1.text: The types of A I nest like boxes. A I is the broad field. Rule-based systems follow rules that people wrote, so they do not learn. Machine learning learns patterns from data instead. Deep learning is machine learning with many-layered neural networks, and it sits behind most vision and language models. Generative A I creates new content, and many generative systems are foundation models. Exam tip: if a question asks for the broadest term, the answer is A I. Machine learning is one way of building it.

1.title: How Machines Learn: Three Approaches
1.text: There are three classic ways a machine learns. Supervised learning uses labeled examples and outputs a label or a value, such as scoring an application as a fit or not. Unsupervised learning uses unlabeled data to find groups, patterns or outliers. Reinforcement learning learns from rewards for its actions, like a robot improving by trial. Self-supervised learning builds its own labels from the data, and it trains many large language models. Exam tip: labels mean supervised, no labels mean unsupervised, rewards mean reinforcement.

1.title: Predictive, Generative and Agentic AI
1.text: Now three kinds by what the system does. Predictive A I scores, classifies or forecasts from past data, like the Helios hiring tool. Generative A I creates new text, images, audio or code, like the Helios assistant. Agentic A I pursues a goal by planning and acting with tools, with few human steps. Narrow A I is built for specific tasks. Artificial general intelligence would match people across tasks, and it is a goal, not what today's laws regulate. Exam tip: general-purpose A I is a legal term for breadth of use. It is not general A I.

1.title: AI Model, AI System, General-Purpose AI
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. An A I model is the trained component, the learned patterns that turn input into output. An A I system puts a model to work, with data flows, an interface, rules and a purpose. Under Article three, point sixty-three, of the E U A I Act, a general-purpose A I model shows significant generality, performs a wide range of distinct tasks competently, and can be built into many downstream systems. Under Article three, point sixty-six, a general-purpose A I system is a system based on such a model. At Helios, the Corvid Labs model is general-purpose, and the support assistant is an A I system.

1.title: The AI Life Cycle Frames the Whole Exam
1.text: The A I life cycle frames the whole exam. The stages are: plan and design, collect data, build and train, test and validate, release, deploy and use, monitor and maintain, and finally retire. Domain three governs development as the developer sees it. Domain four governs deployment and use as the deployer sees it. Risks and duties differ by stage, so policies are written stage by stage. Governance does not stop at release. Exam tip: when a question names a stage, ask who acts at that stage.

1.title: Who Gets Hurt: People, Groups, Organizations, Society
1.text: The Body of Knowledge asks you to identify harms to individuals, groups, organizations and society. Individuals suffer a wrongly rejected application, lost privacy, or physical or psychological harm. Groups suffer discrimination or stereotyping. Organizations suffer disrupted operations, security breaches, monetary loss and damaged reputation. Society suffers weakened democratic participation, unequal access to education, and disinformation at scale. N I S T also counts harm to ecosystems, such as supply chains and the environment. Exam tip: name who bears the harm first. The category follows from the victim.

1.title: Types of Risk: Misalignment, Ethics and Bias, Complexity and Scale
1.text: The Body of Knowledge names three types of risk. Misalignment with objectives means the system optimizes something other than what people intended. For example, the hiring tool might learn to favor the style of past hires instead of job performance. Ethics and bias risk means unfair, discriminatory or intrusive outcomes, such as one group of applicants scoring lower for reasons unrelated to the job. Complexity and scalability means the system is hard to understand, and a single flaw repeats across about twelve thousand applications a quarter. Exam tip: misalignment is a gap between intended and actual objectives.

1.title: Generative AI Adds Its Own Risks
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The N I S T generative A I profile names twelve risks that are unique to, or made worse by, generative A I. Recognize four on sight. Confabulation is confident, false output, often called hallucination. Data privacy is leakage or unauthorized use of personal or sensitive data. Intellectual property is easier copying of protected content. Information integrity covers deepfakes and disinformation at scale. The rest include harmful bias, over-reliance, security, environmental cost and opaque supply chains. Exam tip: hallucination is the popular name. The N I S T term is confabulation.

1.title: Why AI Needs Its Own Governance Approach
1.text: Why does A I need its own governance approach? Traditional software follows logic that people wrote, so the same input gives the same output. A I learns patterns from data, so its outputs are probabilities and can vary. A software failure is a bug to find and fix. An A I failure is an error rate to manage. A I behavior can drift as the data change, so maintenance never ends. And testing is statistical, run on samples. Exam tip: deterministic versus probabilistic output is the contrast the Body of Knowledge itself names.

1.title: Seven Characteristics That Change Governance
1.text: The Body of Knowledge lists seven characteristics that call for a comprehensive approach. Complexity: many components, hard to reason about. Opacity: hard to see why an output was produced. Autonomy: it acts with little or no human step. Speed and scale: decisions come in volume, so errors multiply. Potential for harm or misuse: powerful tools can be turned to bad ends. Data dependency: system quality follows data quality. And probabilistic outputs: likelihoods, not certainties. Exam tip: a question may give a symptom and ask for the characteristic. Match the symptom to the meaning.

1.title: From Characteristic to Governance Response
1.text: Each characteristic points to a governance response. Complexity calls for documentation, expert review and staged testing. Opacity calls for explainability methods, model documentation and disclosure. Autonomy calls for human oversight and limits on what the system may do. Speed and scale call for monitoring, thresholds, and a way to stop the system. Potential for harm or misuse calls for risk assessment, use restrictions and access control. Data dependency calls for data governance. Probabilistic outputs call for error-rate targets and review of edge cases. Exam tip: opacity calls for explanation, autonomy for oversight.

2.title: Responsible AI: The Common Principles
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Six principles recur. Fairness: are people treated equitably? Safety and reliability: does it work as intended without harm? Privacy and security: are data and the system protected? Transparency and explainability: can people see and understand it? Accountability: who answers for the outcome? And human-centricity: does it serve human rights, agency and well-being? Sources use different lists: the O E C D has five principles, the E U has seven ethical principles in Recital twenty-seven, and N I S T has seven characteristics. They overlap heavily. Exam tip: learn the common core.

2.title: Fairness and the Kinds of Bias
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. N I S T names three categories of bias. Systemic bias comes from institutions, norms and society, and it shows up in data and processes; old résumés can carry the pattern of past hiring. Computational and statistical bias comes from non-representative samples or flawed modeling. Human-cognitive bias comes from how people read and use A I output, such as recruiters accepting a score without question. Each can occur with no intent to discriminate, and removing bias does not by itself make a system fair. Exam tip: match the example to the source.

2.title: Safety, Reliability, Privacy and Security
2.text: Safety means the system does not endanger people, property or the environment, in intended use or foreseeable misuse. Reliability means it performs as intended and consistently, including on inputs it did not see in training. Privacy means people keep control of their personal data, and the system collects and infers only what is needed. A I can infer private facts. Security means the system, model and data are protected from attack, theft and misuse. The pairs overlap: an insecure model is also unreliable. Exam tip: safety and reliability ask whether it works without harm.

2.title: Transparency, Explainability and Interpretability
2.text: Three related words, and the exam can separate them. According to N I S T, transparency tells what happened in the system. Explainability tells how a decision was made. Interpretability tells why, and what the output means in context for the user. They support each other. At Helios, applicants are told that A I is used: that is transparency. The recruiter sees which factors drove a score: that is explainability. The recruiter understands what the score means for the role: that is interpretability. Exam tip: what happened, how, why.

2.title: Accountability and Human-Centricity
2.text: Accountability means named people answer for each stage and each outcome. It is not left to the model or the vendor. It needs documentation, decision records, escalation paths and the ability to audit. Human-centricity means A I serves people and respects human rights, agency and well-being. Human oversight is often described in three forms: a person decides, in the loop; a person monitors and can intervene, on the loop; or a person controls whether and how the system is used, in command. At Helios, a recruiter reviews every rejection the tool recommends. Exam tip: a vendor contract does not move accountability away.

2.title: When Principles Pull Apart: Trade-offs
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Principles can pull against each other. N I S T gives three examples: predictive accuracy against interpretability, interpretability against privacy, and privacy-enhancing techniques against accuracy when data are sparse. Analysis can show that a trade-off exists. It cannot tell you how to resolve it. That depends on the context and the values at stake, and the resolution should be transparent and justified. At Helios, a more accurate model that cannot explain itself faces a simpler one that can. Exam tip: the right answer is to decide by context and document why.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. A I is a machine-based system that generates outputs for objectives, and a model, a system and a general-purpose model are different things. The types: machine learning, deep learning, generative and agentic A I, with supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning. The harms fall on individuals, groups, organizations and society. A I needs its own governance because of seven characteristics. And the principles, fairness, safety, privacy, transparency, accountability and human-centricity, can conflict.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Which feature do the O E C D, E U A I Act and N I S T definitions of an A I system have in common? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. All three describe a machine-based or engineered system that generates outputs for objectives. None requires labeled training, full autonomy or a market sale.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Helios finds that its hiring tool gives lower scores to women than to comparable men. Which two harms to people does this show? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. A woman scored down loses a job opportunity, which is harm to an individual, and the pattern is discrimination against a group. The other harms are not shown by the facts.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A team proposes governing a new machine-learning model like any other software release: test it once against a checklist, then leave it unchanged. Which characteristic of A I makes this insufficient? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Outputs are probabilistic and data can drift, so behavior can change after release, and testing and monitoring must continue.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. According to the N I S T A I Risk Management Framework, or R M F, which statement correctly separates transparency, explainability and interpretability? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Transparency tells what happened, explainability tells how a decision was made, and interpretability tells why and what it means to the user. The other orders swap the questions.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. Veridex offers a more accurate ranking model that cannot show why it ranks candidates as it does, and a simpler model that can. Lucia Moreno asks what to do. What is the best answer? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Accuracy and interpretability can trade off. Weigh them for this context, then document and justify the choice.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all five answers. Question one: B. Question two: B and D. Question three: C. Question four: A. Question five: D. That completes Module one. Next, Module two covers governance roles, training and approaches: who does what in an A I governance program.
